## Introduction

In this five-minute demonstration, we will work out what a reader
should cite to find the materials for a particular analysis. We will
inspect the workshop archive and how published GitHub releases can
be archived automatically through the Zenodo integration.

A Git commit identifies a repository revision. A GitHub release gives
a tagged revision a name and a place for release notes and assets.
Zenodo can archive a copy of selected files and issue a DOI. An
archive makes the cited files available under the access conditions
of that record.
[Zenodo records and DOIs](https://help.zenodo.org/docs/deposit/describe-records/reserve-doi/)

## Inspect a record

Open the workshop's archived `v0.2.0` release. Find the creators,
access conditions, and the ZIP of that revision. Compare the Zenodo
version DOI with the GitHub release tag and the concept DOI in
`CITATION.cff`. Cite the version DOI for the files supporting a
result. Cite the concept DOI when referring to the evolving project.
[Version archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24357028) ·
[Concept DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24342489) ·
[GitHub release](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/releases/tag/v0.2.0)

## Connect the website, repository, and archive

The workshop has three connected locations:

| Resource | Role |
| --- | --- |
| [Workshop website](https://jbris.github.io/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/) | Read the published workshop materials. |
| [GitHub repository](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r) | Find the source files, history, and releases used to publish the site. |
| [Zenodo record 24357028](https://zenodo.org/records/24357028) | Find the archived `v0.2.0` release and its version DOI. |

The record's related identifier points to the repository's `v0.2.0`
tag. Follow that link when comparing the archived files with GitHub.
The live website can evolve as the project changes; cite the archived
version that supplied the files for a particular result.

## Automatically archive GitHub releases {#zenodo-github-integration}

For an instructor demonstration or follow-up setup, use Zenodo's
[Enable a repository guide](https://help.zenodo.org/docs/github/enable-repository/):

1. Connect your GitHub account to Zenodo if it is not already linked.
2. In Zenodo's profile menu, select **GitHub**.
3. Select **Sync now** to refresh the list of repositories.
4. Find the repository you maintain and enable its slider. For this
   workshop, inspect the connection for
   `JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r`; use your own repository
   for follow-up practice.
5. Refresh the page and check that the repository is enabled.

Once connected, publishing a new GitHub release triggers automatic
ingestion and archiving in Zenodo. Inspect the resulting version record,
its DOI, metadata, and downloadable files after each release. The
**Sync now** control refreshes the repository list; published releases
are the events that create new archives.

Record `24357028` identifies `v0.2.0`. Later archived releases have
separate version records and DOIs, connected through the project's
version history and concept DOI. Retain the version DOI in the
citation for a specific analysis.

## Decide what to archive

For the `HealthWellbeing` analysis, assemble a candidate list:

-   The exact code revision, pipeline script, and Quarto report source.
-   The report and summary CSV, where upstream terms permit sharing.
-   The lockfile, actual environment record, and container digest if
    the run used a container.
-   The source citation, download URL, checksum, pin version and
    study inclusion rule, plus the relevant metadata and reuse terms.

The upstream download is publicly accessible. Confirm its reuse terms
before including the raw file, pinned copies, or derivatives in a
deposit. If you cannot include a copy, document how an authorised
reader can obtain the source and recreate the selected input. A pin
version identifies an object in a particular board. Preserving a
version identifier with the checksum and filter lets another reader
understand what that object contained.

## Try it yourself

Point to the DOI you would cite for the files you inspected.
Identify one item that would help a reader recreate the precise
version of the input. Explain how you would document its access
conditions. Follow the record's related link to the GitHub tag and
identify the release event that would create the next archive.

## Checkpoint {#zenodo-checkpoint}

You can connect a cited archive to a specific version, distinguish
its DOI from a GitHub release tag, and list the files and metadata
a reader needs. You can explain how an enabled GitHub repository
produces a new Zenodo archive when a release is published. Use the
archive's own citation for the record you inspected and cite the
original review separately for the study data.
